 Letters: Armed Forces ‘represent the best of us’ 
 Readers reflect on Remembrance Day, closer ties with the EU, law changes that could aid police, time change chaos and more 
 A Calgary police officer salutes as the flag-draped coffin of Pte. Aidan Goulding, one or four soldiers killed in the CFB Wainwright fire, passes by in a motorcade on Oct. 29, 2026. Tony D'Andrea writes that we must be forever grateful to the military members who volunteer to defend Canada and accept risks most of us will never know. (Gavin Young / Postmedia) 
 By 
 National Post 
 November 4, 2026 at 6:06 p.m. 
 Last Updated: November 8, 2026 at 8:05 a.m. 
 ‘Canada’s peace and democratic freedom come at a cost’
 Re: Eve n in peacetime, Wainwright tragedy a reminder of the dangers our soldiers face — Bryan Brulotte, Oct. 19 
 Thank you to Bryan Brulotte for his eloquent eulogy to the young soldiers at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright who died while serving, and for reminding us that “the profession of arms demands courage, sacrifice and an acceptance of dangers that most Canadians will never face.”
 The deaths of Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark and Sgt. Morgan Wong — and the terrible injuries suffered by so many others —remind us that the youth who volunteer to defend Canada accept risks most of us will never know.
 We take the cliché “peace, order and good government” for granted. Yet our democratic freedoms depend, in part, on those willing to take up arms in their defence. These emergent men and women serve something greater than themselves: their neighbours, their country and a way of life whose benefits are enjoyed by millions who may never know their names.
 Military service is a conditional life, lived with the knowledge that duty may demand the ultimate sacrifice. These volunteers do not serve primarily for monetary gain, or perhaps even to get an education, but to protect others. Their courage deserves recognition, especially when they serve anonymously and death alone brings their sacrifice to public attention. Such devotion merits public recognition when untimely death occurs.
 They are proof that human nature does not default to selfishness. Their self-sacrifice is life-affirming evidence that we are capable of serving and protecting each other. They represent the best of us: ordinary citizens who accept extraordinary responsibilities. Their exceptional service transcends political differences and leaves us forever indebted to them.
 Canada’s peace and democratic freedom come at a cost. Consequently, on this Remembrance Day, we must honour not only those who fell in past wars but also those who have died in service today. Let flags fly at half-mast. Let bells toll. Let the nation pause in gratitude. Our debt to them deserves special acknowledgement. We should strive to be better citizens to repay that debt and ensure they did not die in vain.
 Tony D’Andrea, Toronto 
 Put EU ties to a vote
 Re: Canada and EU launch ‘Alliance for the Future,’ seeking closer ties — Christopher Nardi, Oct. 30 
 Regardless of political affiliation, Canadians should be asking serious questions about our proposed closer association with the European Union.
 And those questions deserve clear answers from our government. How much of this proposed integration does Canada support? What commitments are being negotiated? Could they restrict the ability of future Canadian governments to make independent decisions?
 And what about Canadians themselves? Where is the public discussion about the implications of such an arrangement?
 Meanwhile, our relationship with the United States remains fundamental to our jobs, manufacturing, trade and economy. Strengthening that relationship deserves urgent attention.
 This is not about Liberals or Conservatives. It is about democratic accountability and Canada’s independence.
 Before accepting commitments that materially affect sovereignty, Canadians deserve a plain-language explanation, full parliamentary scrutiny and meaningful public consultation. Such decisions should be put to a national referendum.
 Canadians deserve to participate in decisions about our country’s future, not simply be told what has already been decided.
 Steve Niedzwiecki, Amaranth, Ont. 
 Change the laws to aid police in arrests
 Re: Amid criticism, Toronto police say they couldn’t arrest Bridle Path suspect at the hospital — Nov. 1 (online) 
 Last Thursday, following an extremely violent home invasion in Toronto’s affluent Bridle Path neighbourhood that seriously injured a family of four, a man who turned out to be one of the three suspects appeared at a local hospital where he presented with a gunshot wound to a shoulder. (Police believe he was accidentally shot by one of his accomplices.) Although police spoke with the suspect at the hospital, he was allowed to leave. Police have stated that they did not have enough evidence to arrest him until a day later, by which time he was long gone.
 I would suggest that all Canadians should be willing to submit to five days of detention if they find themselves under suspicion for a crime they did not commit. This is not an unreasonable price to pay to help the police to do their jobs effectively. Indeed, society could even afford filet mignon and caviar for anyone detained on such suspicions.
 Sometimes, particular crimes become endemic. Drug trafficking is an example. Auto theft, too. And now, home invasions. The Criminal Code should allow for the temporary imposition of special measures to ensure that offenders pay a higher price and that police are afforded an easier time enforcing the related laws.
 Additionally, I note that the Motor Vehicle Act provides penalties for failure to remain at the scene of an “accident” but I have never heard of anyone being charged with failure to remain at the scene of a crime. I have heard of sentences being reduced for criminals who turned themselves in, which is fine, but perhaps there are circumstances in which failure to report a crime or to remain at the scene merits additional punishment. 
 Sean Fraser, Minister of Justice and Attorney General for Canada, has some work to do.
 Patrick Cowan, Toronto 
 Earl Cherniak is a legal hero
 Re: The working theory of legendary lawyer Earl Cherniak — Joseph Brean, Nov. 1 
 I am a retired lawyer who practised law in Sudbury for 45 years. Despite having a lifelong stutter, which I learned to somewhat manage by the time of my early adulthood, I did civil litigation, and did it well enough in my career that I became privileged to receive many referrals from Sudbury colleagues who didn’t do trial work.
 The reason I decided to challenge my speech impediment, and not let it determine my fate, was Earl Cherniak.
 In 1970 he was my first year municipal law professor at the University of Western Ontario’s law school. Within the first minute of his first lecture that year I recognized that he was a person who stuttered. (A stutterer can recognize another stutterer an acoustic mile away.) He managed it well, and never let it deter him from saying exactly what he wanted to say. I was inspired by him. He made me say to myself, “If he can do it, so can I.”
 And I did.
 I know that one of the ways he overcame it was through brilliance and massive pre-trial preparation, which overwhelmed his legal opponents. I know this because a London lawyer I had a case with told me how the London Bar was in awe of Mr. Cherniak’s trial preparation, legal abilities and courtroom skills.
 Years later, the Law Society of Ontario opened a file on me as a result of my book, There is no Difference: An Argument for the Abolition of the Indian Reserve System and Special Race-based Laws and Entitlements for Canada’s Indians. The society suggested it had “good reason to believe” that my book, which argues for complete legal equality between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Canadians, “brought the administration of justice into disrepute.”
 The illustrious Barbara Kay published a column in this paper defending me and excoriating the Law Society.
 The same day the column was published I received an unsolicited email from Mr. Cherniak, who did not know me or know that I had been a former student of his.
 He was outraged that our Law Society was investigating me and offered to defend me in any proceedings they brought.
 In email exchanges I was able to tell him and thank him for the example he gave me of courage and stubbornness in the face of what one might think was an impediment that disqualified one from any profession involving public speaking.
 Earl Cherniak will always be a legal and personal hero to me. He represents the very best that a lawyer should be, both in the courts and in society in general.
 Peter Best, Sudbury 
 A time of our choosing
 Re: Parts of Florida and B.C now on the same time — Nov. 2 
 The Parti Québécois government wishes to abolish the semi-annual clock change — a move supported by a majority of Quebecers. But which option should be chosen: standard time or daylight saving time (also known as summer time)?
 Professionals argue that standard time is better for our health, while the business community leans toward the latter, claiming it boosts commerce.
 Our neighbours to the south, as well as Ontario, will likely opt for daylight saving time — prioritizing business. Quebec, however, should assert its independence and put health before business. Let’s embrace standard time!
 Who knows? If we abolish the clock change and permanently adopt standard time before our immediate neighbours take action, they might just follow our lead. Let’s take the initiative. The clock is ticking.
 Sylvio Le Blanc, Montreal 
 Black market for vaping products thriving
 Re: Ottawa and provinces losing billions from illegal cigarettes, study finds — Simon Tuck , Nov. 2 
 Simon Tuck reports that governments have lost billions in excise tax revenue due to contraband tobacco. As the president of the Canadian Vaping Association (CVA), I would like to note that these findings serve as a clear warning about what is happening in Canada’s vaping market today.
 When governments make legal products less affordable, the illicit market thrives. High excise taxes, flavour restrictions and inadequate enforcement have created opportunities for illegal operators while legal businesses struggle to compete. 
 Recent research by Concordia University economist Ian Irvine estimates that illicit products now account for nearly 30 per cent of Canada’s vaping market. 
 These products operate outside regulatory oversight, with no nicotine limits, ingredient disclosure, safety standards or age-verification requirements. 
 Yet despite this, Canada’s tobacco-control lobbyists continue to push for a nationwide flavour ban, while the CVA consistently calls for stronger enforcement, tougher penalties for repeat offenders, and youth protections that do not punish responsible adult consumers or compliant businesses.
 The illicit cigarette crisis did not happen overnight. Neither did the growing availability of illegal vaping products. Governments must not continue introducing overly restrictive policies without fully evaluating the risks to public health and safety. 
 The answer isn’t prohibition. It’s smarter regulation, proportionate taxation, and enforcement that works. 
 Sam Tam, President, Canadian Vaping Association
